summary:
**ORBIT-X – Space Mission Design & Simulation**

ORBIT-X is an interactive 3D space mission design and simulation platform that makes aerospace engineering concepts accessible through an immersive, hands-on experience. It allows users to design and configure spacecraft by selecting structural components, propulsion systems, fuel, power systems, communication equipment, and scientific instruments while managing mass, power consumption, and mission budgets.

The platform guides users through spacecraft validation, launch preparation, rocket launch simulation, stage separation, orbital insertion, and mission operations. It features three progressive missions: Lunar Explorer, Earth Observer, and Mars Pathfinder. Real-time flight telemetry, mission objectives, performance analysis, and an AI-powered assistant help users understand engineering decisions and correct design mistakes.

ORBIT-X addresses the challenge of making complex space mission concepts easier to explore, understand, and simulate through an engaging, educational 3D environment.
details: ORBIT-X is an interactive, science-first space-mission design game. Players choose Lunar Explorer, Earth Observer, or Mars Pathfinder, then build a spacecraft from modular structure, propulsion, propellant, power, communications, and science-instrument components. Live engineering indicators show how mass, cost, power balance, payload fit, and delta-v change with each design decision. Players validate a launch vehicle, follow a 3D launch and telemetry timeline, manage mission anomalies, make operational decisions, and receive a scored debrief. A shared-screen hot-seat mode supports up to four team roles, while password-free judge routes let reviewers explore mission stages and selected failure scenarios. ORBIT-X was built with React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Three.js, React Three Fiber, and Zustand, with optional Supabase cloud sync and a Gemini-powered flight advisor. NASA imagery, 3D assets, and published mission and planetary references ground selected visuals and model checks. The intended impact is to make spacecraft engineering trade-offs more understandable to students and educators through hands-on experimentation. The simulation is educational, not engineering-certified: ascent follows a reference telemetry spline, orbits are simplified, and radio links use a simplified link budget.
